citations.quote:
The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$

derivations.claim: For any Lebesgue-integrable vector function $h$ with $\int\|h\|_2<\infty$, write $I=\int h$. If $I=0$, the norm inequality is immediate. Otherwise put $q=I/\|I\|_2$. Then $\|I\|_2=\int q^Th\le\int|q^Th|\le\int\|h\|_2$, by [F1], linearity componentwise, and $\|q\|_2=1$. Thus the vector integral estimate needed below holds for these Lebesgue integrands. Now put $g=Bu\in L^1(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$; this follows from $B\in L^\infty$, $u\in L^2$, and [F5]. Choose a finite partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ with $\|A\|_\infty(t_{j+1}-t_j)<1$ on each subinterval when $\|A\|_\infty>0$; if $\|A\|_\infty=0$, use $N=1$. Given the already constructed value $x(t_j)$, define $\mathcal T z(t)=x(t_j)+\int_{t_j}^t(A(s)z(s)+g(s))ds$ on $C([t_j,t_{j+1}];\mathbb R^n)$. By [F2], $\mathcal T$ maps continuous functions to continuous functions, and the vector-integral estimate just proved gives $\|\mathcal T z-\mathcal T w\|_\infty\le q_j\|z-w\|_\infty$ with $q_j=\|A\|_\infty(t_{j+1}-t_j)<1$.

Starting from the constant function $z_0=x(t_j)$, let $z_{k+1}=\mathcal T z_k$. Then $\|z_{k+1}-z_k\|_\infty\le q_j^k\|z_1-z_0\|_\infty$, so the successive differences have summable norms. Each coordinate converges uniformly by [F3], and the finite coordinate limit is a continuous vector function $z$. The integral estimate in step 1.1 makes $\mathcal T$ continuous in the supremum norm, hence $z=\mathcal Tz$. If $z,w$ are two fixed points, $\|z-w\|_\infty\le q_j\|z-w\|_\infty$, so $z=w$. Solving the finitely many subintervals in order gives one continuous solution on $[0,T]$, and the same uniqueness on each subinterval proves global uniqueness.

The integrand $Ax+Bu$ lies in $L^1$. Its indefinite integral is absolutely continuous by [F2], as required in the Statement. Under [A1], the $L^1$ fundamental theorem in [F2] differentiates the integral equation almost everywhere and yields $\dot x=Ax+Bu$. The same equation is independent of the chosen representatives of $A,B,u$ by [F6].

From the integral equation and step 1.1, $\|x(t)\|_2\le \|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1}+\|A\|_\infty\int_0^t\|x(s)\|_2ds$. Apply [F4] with $c=\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u\|_{L^1}$ and then [F5]; this gives the displayed supremum bound.

Linearity of the integral [F6] shows that a linear combination of two zero-initial-state solutions is the solution for the same linear combination of controls; uniqueness from step 2.1 makes the zero-initial-state map linear. Step 3.2 with $x_0=0$ bounds this linear map in the $L^2$ and supremum norms, while the fixed initial-state contribution is independent of $u$. Hence the full map is affine and bounded as claimed.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. Let $I$ be a nonempty directed preorder and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ a net in $X$ ([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). For $x\in X$, write $x_i\rightharpoonup x$ and say the net **converges weakly to $x$** when it converges to $x$ in $\sigma(X,X^*)$ ([[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]], [[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). Equivalently,

$$\forall f\in X^*\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\in I\ \forall i\ge i_0:\quad |f(x_i)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.$$

Indeed, topological convergence implies each of these eventual conditions because the inverse disk is a neighborhood. Conversely, a neighborhood contains a finite intersection of inverse scalar neighborhoods containing $x$. Coordinate convergence gives an eventual index for each of the finitely many conditions; directedness gives a common upper bound for them, after which the whole intersection contains the net. For the empty intersection use any index of the nonempty $I$. This proves the equivalence without a choice axiom.

A **weakly convergent sequence** is this definition with $I=\mathbb N$ in its usual order. A constant net converges weakly to its value, including in the zero space. The specified limit must be a point of $X$; without a separation hypothesis uniqueness is not part of the definition. Weak closure continues to mean topological closure, not merely the set of limits of sequences.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, and give $\mathbb{R}$ its usual topology,
the metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Let

$$\mathbb{R}^n \;=\; \prod_{k < n} \mathbb{R}$$

be the product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]). As a
**set** this is literally the $\mathbb{R}^n$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], both being
the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$; and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the
three metrics defined there. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the metric topology of $d_\infty$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]). The key computation is that a $d_\infty$-ball is a
   box:
   $$B_{d_\infty}(x, r) \;=\; \prod_{k<n} (x_k - r,\ x_k + r) \qquad (r > 0),$$
   a product of bounded open intervals ([[def-interval]]).
2. $d_\infty \le d_1 \le n\, d_\infty$ and $d_\infty \le d_2 \le n\, d_\infty$
   pointwise, so $d_1$ and $d_2$ are each Lipschitz equivalent to $d_\infty$
   ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]); here $n$ denotes the canonical natural
   $n \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$.
3. Consequently all three metrics induce the product topology
   ([[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]]). So $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the product
   topology and $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the topology of any one of $d_1$, $d_2$,
   $d_\infty$ are **one topological space**, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** The metric $d_\infty$ is a maximum over $n$ terms, which does

derivations.claim: For $q\in\mathbb R^m$ set $h(q)=\sup_{c\in U_c}q^Tc$, which is finite because $U_c$ is compact and hence bounded. If $z\notin U_c$, [F3] gives a nearest point $y\in U_c$ to $z$. For each $c\in U_c$ and $0<\theta\le1$, convexity gives $y+\theta(c-y)\in U_c$; minimality of $y$ implies $\|z-y-\theta(c-y)\|_2^2\ge\|z-y\|_2^2$, and division by $\theta$ followed by $\theta\downarrow0$ gives $(z-y)^T(c-y)\le0$. Thus $q_0=z-y$ satisfies $q_0^Tz-h(q_0)\ge\|z-y\|_2^2>0$. If $M_c=\sup_{c\in U_c}\|c\|_2$, then $|h(q)-h(q_0)|\le M_c\|q-q_0\|_2$ and $|(q-q_0)^Tz|\le\|q-q_0\|_2\|z\|_2$. Rational vectors are dense in $\mathbb R^m$, so one can choose rational $q$ close enough to $q_0$ that $q^Tz>h(q)$. Therefore a point $z$ belongs to $U_c$ exactly when $q^Tz\le h(q)$ for every rational vector $q$.

Fix a rational $q$. Every $u_k$ is in $\mathcal U_c$, so $h(q)-q^Tu_k(t)\ge0$ almost everywhere. For any measurable $E\subseteq[0,T]$, the test function $q\mathbf1_E$ lies in $L^2$ because $T<\infty$; weak convergence, [F2], and [F4] give $\int_Eq^Tu\,dt=\lim_k\int_Eq^Tu_k\,dt\le h(q)|E|$. If $q^Tu>h(q)$ on a set of positive measure, then for some integer $r\ge1$ the measurable set $E_r=\{t:q^Tu(t)\ge h(q)+1/r\}$ has positive measure, contradicting the integral inequality with $E=E_r$. Hence $q^Tu(t)\le h(q)$ almost everywhere.

The rational vectors form a countable set, so the exceptional null sets from step 1.2 have a null union. Outside that union all rational support inequalities hold simultaneously; step 1.1 then gives $u(t)\in U_c$ almost everywhere. This is exactly $u\in\mathcal U_c$.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. Let $I$ be a nonempty directed preorder and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ a net in $X$ ([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). For $x\in X$, write $x_i\rightharpoonup x$ and say the net **converges weakly to $x$** when it converges to $x$ in $\sigma(X,X^*)$ ([[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]], [[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). Equivalently,

$$\forall f\in X^*\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\in I\ \forall i\ge i_0:\quad |f(x_i)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.$$

Indeed, topological convergence implies each of these eventual conditions because the inverse disk is a neighborhood. Conversely, a neighborhood contains a finite intersection of inverse scalar neighborhoods containing $x$. Coordinate convergence gives an eventual index for each of the finitely many conditions; directedness gives a common upper bound for them, after which the whole intersection contains the net. For the empty intersection use any index of the nonempty $I$. This proves the equivalence without a choice axiom.

A **weakly convergent sequence** is this definition with $I=\mathbb N$ in its usual order. A constant net converges weakly to its value, including in the zero space. The specified limit must be a point of $X$; without a separation hypothesis uniqueness is not part of the definition. Weak closure continues to mean topological closure, not merely the set of limits of sequences.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], the states have a common bound $M_x$ in supremum norm. For $s,t\in[0,T]$, the integral equation and [F4] give $\|x_{u_k}(t)-x_{u_k}(s)\|_2\le L|t-s|$, where $L:=\|A\|_\infty M_x+\|B\|_\infty M_c$. The same bound holds for $x_u$.
For each fixed $t$, evaluation at $t$ composed with the bounded linear zero-initial-state map in [F1] is a bounded linear functional on $L^2$. Thus [F3] gives $x_{u_k}(t)\to x_u(t)$ coordinatewise.

If $L=0$, step 1.1 makes each state constant, and step 1.2 gives uniform convergence. If $L>0$, fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose a finite partition of $[0,T]$ with mesh smaller than $\varepsilon/(3L)$. By step 1.2 and finiteness of its nodes, there is an index after which $\|x_{u_k}-x_u\|_2<\varepsilon/3$ at every node. Any $t$ is within the mesh of a node, so step 1.1 gives $\|x_{u_k}(t)-x_u(t)\|_2\le L|t-t_j|+\|x_{u_k}(t_j)-x_u(t_j)\|_2+L|t-t_j|<\varepsilon$. Hence the convergence is uniform.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].
For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], if $u_k,u\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $x_{u_k}\to x_u$ uniformly on $[0,T]$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the weak limit $u$ belongs to $\mathcal U_c$, so [F2] applies. Put $e_k=x_{u_k}-x_d$ and $e=x_u-x_d$; their difference $e_k-e=x_{u_k}-x_u$ tends to zero uniformly. Since $Q$ is essentially bounded, the estimate $|a^TQ(t)a-b^TQ(t)b|\le\|Q(t)\|_2(\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2)\|a-b\|_2$ shows that $\int_0^T e_k^TQe_k\,dt\to\int_0^T e^TQe\,dt$. The terminal terms converge by the same estimate with $P$ and $x_{u_k}(T)\to x_u(T)$.

Let $\mathscr Rv=R(\cdot)v(\cdot)$. The bounds on $R$ imply $\|\mathscr Rv\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ and $\langle\mathscr Rv,v\rangle\ge0$; symmetry gives $\langle\mathscr Rv,w\rangle=\langle v,\mathscr Rw\rangle$. For every fixed $w\in L^2$, $\langle\mathscr Ru_k,u_k\rangle\ge2\langle\mathscr Ru_k,w\rangle-\langle\mathscr Rw,w\rangle$, because the difference is $\langle\mathscr R(u_k-w),u_k-w\rangle\ge0$. The right-hand side converges to $2\langle\mathscr Ru,w\rangle-\langle\mathscr Rw,w\rangle$ by weak convergence, as [F3] makes $v\mapsto\langle\mathscr Rv,w\rangle=\langle v,\mathscr Rw\rangle$ bounded. Taking the supremum over $w$ gives $\liminf_k\langle\mathscr Ru_k,u_k\rangle\ge\langle\mathscr Ru,u\rangle$, with equality in the supremum at $w=u$.

The state and terminal cost terms converge by step 1.1, while the control quadratic term is lower semicontinuous by step 1.2. Multiplying by $1/2$ and adding these three terms gives $J(u)\le\liminf_k J(u_k)$.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is a curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ whose coordinates are absolutely continuous in the scalar sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $a\le b$.

1. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is absolutely continuous and $F'=0$ almost everywhere on $(a,b)$, then $F$ is constant.
2. Let $n\ge1$, let $y:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ have absolutely continuous coordinates, and let $h\in L^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)$. If $y'_j=h_j$ almost everywhere for each coordinate $j$, then, for every $t\in[a,b]$,
$$y(t)=y(a)+\int_a^t h(s)\,ds.$$
Here $h\in L^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)$ means that each coordinate $h_j$ is Lebesgue integrable, and the integral is the componentwise Lebesgue integral. For $a=b$ it is zero.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: The forcing $g(s):=Q(T-s)(x_u(T-s)-x_d(T-s))$ lies in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$: $Q$ is essentially bounded, $x_u$ is continuous on a compact interval and hence bounded, and $x_d\in L^2$. Also $C(s):=A(T-s)^T\in L^\infty$. Apply [F1] with $D(s)=I$ and initial value $q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$ to obtain an absolutely continuous $q$ satisfying the forward Volterra integral equation and $\dot q=Cq+g$ almost everywhere.

Set $p(t)=q(T-t)$. Time reversal preserves absolute continuity, and differentiating almost everywhere gives $-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))$ with $p(T)=q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$. Thus $p$ satisfies [F2].

If $\widetilde p$ is another adjoint solution, time reversal gives an absolutely continuous $\widetilde q(s)=\widetilde p(T-s)$ with $\widetilde q(0)=q(0)$ and $\dot{\widetilde q}=C\widetilde q+g$ almost everywhere. By [F4], $\widetilde q$ is continuous and bounded componentwise. Since $C\in L^\infty$, $g\in L^2$ and [F5] gives $g\in L^1$, the function $h=C\widetilde q+g$ belongs to $L^1$ componentwise. Apply [F3] to obtain $\widetilde q(s)=q(0)+\int_0^s(C(r)\widetilde q(r)+g(r))\,dr$ for every $s$. This is exactly the forward Volterra equation used to construct $q$ in step 1.1. Its actual integral-equation uniqueness in [F1] gives $\widetilde q=q$, hence $\widetilde p=p$.

citations.quote:
The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every real or complex Hilbert space $H$ is reflexive: the canonical evaluation map $J_H:H\to H^{**}$ is surjective.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC and HB. Let $X$ be a real reflexive Banach space ([[def-reflexive-banach-space]]), let $A\subseteq X$ be nonempty and weakly sequentially closed ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]), and let $I:A\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, coercive on $A$ and weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous on $A$ ([[def-proper-coercive-and-weakly-lower-semicontinuous-functional]]). Then $I$ attains its infimum on $A$: there exists $u_0\in A$ with $I(u_0)=\inf_A I$. The admissible set may be taken convex and norm closed in $X$, by [[thm-norm-closed-convex-iff-weakly-closed]].

Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex, and let $\mathcal U_c$ be the pointwise admissible set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]]. If $u_k\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in real $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $u\in\mathcal U_c$. Thus $\mathcal U_c$ is weakly sequentially closed.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].
For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], if $u_k\in\mathcal U_c$ and $u_k\rightharpoonup u$ weakly in $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, then $J(u)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}J(u_k)$.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F3], Countable Choice is available. Hence [F1] makes $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ a real Hilbert space and [F2] makes it reflexive.

The set $\mathcal F$ is nonempty by hypothesis and weakly sequentially closed by [F5]. For $u\in\mathcal F$, every state and terminal quadratic term in $J$ is nonnegative, while $R(t)\succeq rI$ gives $J(u)\ge\tfrac r2\|u\|_2^2$. The cost is finite on $\mathcal F$ by [F7], so $J$ is proper and coercive there.

By [F6], $J$ is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous on $\mathcal F$. The axioms in [A1] and the reflexivity and admissibility checks in steps 1.1–1.2 verify every hypothesis of [F4]; therefore there exists $u^*\in\mathcal F$ with $J(u^*)=\inf_{u\in\mathcal F}J(u)$.

The state map is affine by [F7]. For $0<\theta<1$, each positive-semidefinite quadratic state or terminal form satisfies $q(\theta a+(1-\theta)b)=\theta q(a)+(1-\theta)q(b)-\theta(1-\theta)q(a-b)\le\theta q(a)+(1-\theta)q(b)$. The control form satisfies $\frac12\langle R(\theta u+(1-\theta)v),\theta u+(1-\theta)v\rangle=\frac\theta2\langle Ru,u\rangle+\frac{1-\theta}2\langle Rv,v\rangle-\frac{\theta(1-\theta)}2\langle R(u-v),u-v\rangle$. If $u\ne v$, then $\langle R(u-v),u-v\rangle\ge r\|u-v\|_2^2>0$, so $J$ is strictly convex on the convex set $\mathcal F$. Two distinct minimizers would have a feasible strict convex combination with smaller cost, contradicting the minimum value established in step 2.1. Thus $u^*$ is unique.

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\|A\|_\infty$ and $\|B\|_\infty$ for the essential suprema of their Euclidean operator norms. There is a unique absolutely continuous $x:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$$
x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
Under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot x=A x+B u$ almost everywhere, and it always satisfies
$$
\|x\|_\infty\le e^{\|A\|_\infty T}\left(\|x_0\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\sqrt T\,\|u\|_2\right).
$$
For fixed $A,B,x_0$, the map $u\mapsto x_u$ is affine into $C([0,T];\mathbb R^n)$, and its zero-initial-state linear part is bounded from $L^2$ to the supremum norm.

The almost-everywhere derivative assertion uses Countable Choice, as required by the cited $L^1$ fundamental theorem. The integral-equation existence, uniqueness, bound, and affine-map claims do not require that axiom.

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is a curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ whose coordinates are absolutely continuous in the scalar sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

For every LQR data set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and every admissible control $u$, the adjoint in [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]] exists and is unique.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the state variation $\delta x=x_{u+w}-x$ is linear in $w$ and satisfies $\|\delta x\|_\infty\le C_0\|w\|_2$ for a fixed constant $C_0$. Expanding the running and terminal quadratic forms gives the linear term $\int_0^T (x-x_d)^TQ\delta x\,dt+\int_0^T u^TRw\,dt+(x(T)-x_T)^TP\delta x(T)$ and a remainder $\frac12\int_0^T(\delta x^TQ\delta x+w^TRw)dt+\frac12\delta x(T)^TP\delta x(T)$. Boundedness of $Q,R,P$ and the state-map estimate bound this remainder by $C\|w\|_2^2$. Thus the displayed linear term is the first-order norm derivative before rewriting its state contributions through the adjoint.

Apply [F3] to $p$ and $\delta x$, whose absolute continuity follows from [F1] and [F2]. Using their differential equations gives $p(T)^T\delta x(T)-p(0)^T\delta x(0)=-\int_0^T(x-x_d)^TQ\delta x\,dt+\int_0^T p^TBw\,dt$. Since $\delta x(0)=0$ and $p(T)=P(x(T)-x_T)$, rearranging yields $\int_0^T(x-x_d)^TQ\delta x\,dt+(x(T)-x_T)^TP\delta x(T)=\int_0^T p^TBw\,dt$.

Substitute the identity from step 1.2 into the derivative coefficient of step 1.1 and use $(p^TBw)=(B^Tp)^Tw$ and $(u^TRw)=(Ru)^Tw$ because $R=R^T$ almost everywhere. The resulting coefficient is $DJ(u)[w]$. Moreover, $B^Tp+Ru\in L^2$ since $B,R$ are essentially bounded, $p$ is continuous, and $u\in L^2$; [F4] therefore makes $DJ(u)$ a bounded linear map. The quadratic remainder bound in step 1.1 proves the stated first-order norm expansion.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For the LQR problem of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], let $u\in\mathcal U_c$, let $x=x_u$, and let $p$ be its adjoint from [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]]. Define the bounded linear map $DJ(u):L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)\to\mathbb R$ by
$$DJ(u)[w]=\int_0^T\big(B(t)^Tp(t)+R(t)u(t)\big)^Tw(t)\,dt.$$
It is the first-order norm derivative of $J$ at $u$ in the precise sense that $J(u+w)-J(u)-DJ(u)[w]=O(\|w\|_2^2)$ as $\|w\|_2\to0$.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, state and control dimensions $n,m\ge1$, and the real quotient space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$ of measurable controls modulo equality almost everywhere ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Let $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$ be equivalence classes, let $x_0,x_T\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $x_d\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^n)$. Let $U_c\subset\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, compact and convex. The pointwise control set is
$$
\mathcal U_c:=\{u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m):u(t)\in U_c\text{ for almost every }t\}.
$$
Let $Q\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$ and $R\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{m\times m})$ be symmetric almost everywhere, with $Q(t)\succeq0$ and $rI\preceq R(t)\preceq MI$ almost everywhere for constants $0<r\le M<\infty$. Let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite. For each $u\in\mathcal U_c$, its state is the unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$$
x_u(t)=x_0+\int_0^t\big(A(s)x_u(s)+B(s)u(s)\big)\,ds.
$$
The same state equation is defined for every $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and the running and terminal cost on that ambient space is
$$
J(u)=\frac12\int_0^T\!\left((x_u(t)-x_d(t))^TQ(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t))+u(t)^TR(t)u(t)\right)dt+\frac12(x_u(T)-x_T)^TP(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$
The constrained problem minimizes this ambient functional over $\mathcal F$, where additional path or terminal constraints are represented by a nonempty convex weakly sequentially closed set $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U_c$; with no additional state constraints, $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. “Weakly sequentially closed” means that every weakly convergent sequence in $\mathcal F$ has its weak limit in $\mathcal F$ ([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]). The definition asserts no optimizer or adjoint existence; the state-map well-definedness is supplied by [[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]].

Let $T>0$, $A\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times n})$, $B\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathbb R^{n\times m})$, $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, and give $\mathbb{R}$ its usual topology,
the metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Let

$$\mathbb{R}^n \;=\; \prod_{k < n} \mathbb{R}$$

be the product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]). As a
**set** this is literally the $\mathbb{R}^n$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], both being
the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$; and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the
three metrics defined there. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the metric topology of $d_\infty$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]). The key computation is that a $d_\infty$-ball is a
   box:
   $$B_{d_\infty}(x, r) \;=\; \prod_{k<n} (x_k - r,\ x_k + r) \qquad (r > 0),$$
   a product of bounded open intervals ([[def-interval]]).
2. $d_\infty \le d_1 \le n\, d_\infty$ and $d_\infty \le d_2 \le n\, d_\infty$
   pointwise, so $d_1$ and $d_2$ are each Lipschitz equivalent to $d_\infty$
   ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]); here $n$ denotes the canonical natural
   $n \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$.
3. Consequently all three metrics induce the product topology
   ([[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]]). So $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the product
   topology and $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the topology of any one of $d_1$, $d_2$,
   $d_\infty$ are **one topological space**, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** The metric $d_\infty$ is a maximum over $n$ terms, which does
not exist for $n = 0$; [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries the same hypothesis, and it
is carried here for the same reason. For $n = 0$ the product is a one-point space
and there is nothing to compare.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $u$ minimizes $J$ on $\mathcal F$ and fix $v\in\mathcal F$. Convexity gives $u_\theta=u+\theta(v-u)\in\mathcal F$ for $0\le\theta\le1$. Hence $(J(u_\theta)-J(u))/\theta\ge0$ for $0<\theta\le1$. The first-order expansion [F1] with increment $\theta(v-u)$ has quotient $DJ(u)[v-u]+O(\theta\|v-u\|_2^2)$, so its limit is $DJ(u)[v-u]$. This proves the displayed variational inequality.

Suppose the pointwise inequalities hold outside one null set and $\mathcal F=\mathcal U_c$. For any $v\in\mathcal U_c$, substitute $c=v(t)$ outside that null set and the null set on which $v(t)\notin U_c$. The vector $g=B^Tp+Ru$ lies in $L^2$ because $B,R$ are essentially bounded, $p$ is continuous on the compact horizon, and $u\in L^2$; [F3] makes $g^T(v-u)$ integrable. Integrating proves the global variational inequality.

Assume the variational inequality at $u$. For any $v\in\mathcal F$, [F2] and $Q\succeq0$, $R\succeq rI$ give $J(v)-J(u)\ge DJ(u)[v-u]+\frac r2\|v-u\|_2^2$. The linear term is nonnegative by the assumed inequality; hence $J(v)\ge J(u)$, with strict inequality if $v\ne u$. Thus $u$ is the unique minimizer.

Assume the global variational inequality and suppose no common null set makes all pointwise inequalities true. Construct a countable dense $D\subseteq U_c$ by choosing, using [A1], one point from each rational open ball that meets $U_c$; the countable base property makes the chosen set dense. Define $M=\bigcup_{d\in D,k\ge1}E_{d,k}$, where $E_{d,k}=\{t:g(t)^T(d-u(t))\le-1/k\}$. This is measurable. Continuity in $c$ and density show that $M$ is exactly the set where some $c\in U_c$ violates the pointwise inequality, so the absence of a common null set means $|M|>0$. Countability implies some $E_{d,k}$ has positive measure. Put $v(t)=d$ on that set and $v(t)=u(t)$ elsewhere. This measurable control lies in $\mathcal U_c$, but $\int_0^Tg^T(v-u)dt\le-|E_{d,k}|/k<0$, contradicting the assumed global variational inequality. Therefore one null set suffices for every $c\in U_c$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

For the data of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and an admissible control $u$ with state $x_u$, a **continuous LQR adjoint** is a curve $p:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n$ whose coordinates are absolutely continuous in the scalar sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], satisfying, almost everywhere,
$$
-\dot p(t)=A(t)^Tp(t)+Q(t)(x_u(t)-x_d(t)),\qquad p(T)=P(x_u(T)-x_T).
$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For the LQR problem of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], let $u\in\mathcal U_c$, let $x=x_u$, and let $p$ be its adjoint from [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]]. Define the bounded linear map $DJ(u):L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^m)\to\mathbb R$ by
$$DJ(u)[w]=\int_0^T\big(B(t)^Tp(t)+R(t)u(t)\big)^Tw(t)\,dt.$$
It is the first-order norm derivative of $J$ at $u$ in the precise sense that $J(u+w)-J(u)-DJ(u)[w]=O(\|w\|_2^2)$ as $\|w\|_2\to0$.

derivations.claim: For every feasible $u$, [F1] applied to $u\ge0$ and $\int_0^1u=0$ gives $u=0$ almost everywhere. Thus $\mathcal F=\{0\}$ and $u^*=0$ is its unique feasible control and hence a minimizer.
The state is $x(t)=0$. The adjoint equation becomes $-\dot p=-1$ with $p(1)=0$, whose unique solution is $p(t)=t-1$. The reduced gradient at $u^*$ is therefore $g(t)=p(t)=t-1$.

For the pointwise control-only condition, choose the admissible point $c=1$. Then $g(t)(c-u^*(t))=t-1<0$ for every $t\in[0,1)$, a set of positive measure. Hence the asserted pointwise condition fails, although the global variational inequality over the singleton $\mathcal F$ holds with equality.

For the direct linear-stage branch, optionally supply exact pointwise coefficient maps $A:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $B:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ satisfying $f(t,x,u)=A(t)x+B(t)u$ at every queried stage input; only this explicit representation enables that branch. Supply a deterministic derivative evaluator for the actual returned stage maps and resulting finite NLP on an open neighborhood of the queried candidate. On a locally fixed strict stopping branch of the finite stage-iteration procedure, differentiate that finite graph, including when the residual happens to be exactly zero at the queried point. Implicit differentiation as in [[thm-implicit-differentiation-forward-and-adjoint-formulas]] is permitted only when the selected returned stage map is certified to agree on that neighborhood with the exact local solution branch and its residual Jacobian is nonsingular there; an exact residual at the queried point alone does not establish this agreement. Return `derivative-failure` when no derivative of the actual returned map is available. Supply a quadrature error evaluator which returns a certified upper bound for the objective quadrature discrepancy or `unavailable`. Each supplied evaluator returns a value or failure in finite time. An optional trajectory-estimation request supplies the inputs of [[alg-bounded-adaptive-runge-kutta-controller]].
$$X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_{k<i}a_{ik}F_{j,k},\quad t_{j,i}=t_j+c_ih_j,\quad F_{j,i}=f(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j),\quad \Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iF_{j,i}.$$

**Mesh and constraints.** Check that the original mesh satisfies $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ and that all declared constraint and quadrature times lie in $[0,T]$; if either check fails, return `mesh-domain-failure` without evaluation. If the original node count exceeds the supplied cap, return `mesh-budget-exhausted`. Insert every declared path-constraint time not already a node, unless this exceeds the node cap, in which case return `mesh-budget-exhausted`. Tie each inserted subcell's control to its original containing cell, so the parameterization is unchanged. On the resulting mesh, check all stage times $t_j+c_i h_j$ lie in $[0,T]$ before querying $f$ or $L$; an invalid time returns `mesh-domain-failure` with no evaluation. Each tableau stage and its quadrature contribution use the control $u_j$ of that cell, as in the stage equations below. At a declared path- or endpoint-constraint time that is a mesh node before $T$, use the right-hand original-cell value from the half-open representative in [[def-ctrl1-control-mesh-and-piecewise-constant-parameterization]]; at $T$, use the last original-cell control value unless a separate endpoint-control variable is supplied. Use the same convention at separately declared non-stage quadrature times. An endpoint constraint is evaluated at its declared endpoint. This is finite sampling and does not assert continuous-path feasibility.

**Stage evaluation.** On each cell write $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$ and $u_j$ for its tied constant control. Before forming any stages, check $X_{j,0}\in\Omega_x$ and $u_j\in\Omega_u$; a failed check returns `stage-domain-failure` with the cell and no objective candidate. For an explicit tableau, form the stages recursively by the displayed equations. Before each query of $f$ or $L$, check that the time is in $[0,T]$, the state lies in $\Omega_x$, and the control lies in $\Omega_u$; a failed membership check returns `stage-domain-failure`, and an unavailable function value returns `stage-evaluation-failure` with the cell and stage index. For an implicit tableau, do not leave the collocation stages as outer NLP decision variables. Form the coupled slope residual
$$R_j(K;X_{j,0},u_j)_i=K_i-f\!\left(t_j+c_ih_j,X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k,u_j\right),\quad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

A failed domain check returns `stage-domain-failure` with the failing cell and stage index, the partial result record, and no objective candidate. If all checks pass, the exact solution of $M_jK=r$ is the stage vector and the nonlinear-solve status is `exact-linear-stage-solve`. derivations.claim: Given any control tuple feasible in single shooting, calculate $X_{1,0}=\Phi_0(x_0,u_0)$, then each later $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. Uniqueness of each deterministic map makes this recursively defined state tuple well-defined; by construction it satisfies every multiple-shooting continuity equation.

Conversely, a multiple-shooting feasible tuple has fixed $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and satisfies each continuity equation. Induction on $j$ forces its $X_{j,0}$ to equal the recursive single-shooting value for the same controls. Hence there is exactly one multiple-shooting state tuple for each feasible control tuple and the projection is bijective.

Under this bijection the states at all shared nodes agree. Therefore every node constraint has the same value and every objective formed from the same node/stage values is identical. Thus reduced feasibility and objective values coincide.

supplier_interfaces.required_hypotheses: [F1] An interval map is available only after its explicit stages or implicit stage residual solve return a successful status; it assigns exactly one deterministic endpoint to that successful start/control pair, and single shooting applies it recursively ([[alg-ctrl1-runge-kutta-shooting-and-collocation-transcription]]).
[F2] The multiple-shooting variables satisfy $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$ ([[alg-ctrl1-runge-kutta-shooting-and-collocation-transcription]]).

The common initial state and final endpoint are retained.
