citations.quote: For the horizon $[0,T]$ of [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]], a time mesh is a finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ with $N\ge1$. Its cell widths are $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j>0$ and its mesh size is $|\Delta|=\max_{0\le j<N}h_j$. A piecewise-constant control vector is $(u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1})$ and represents the measurable control $u^\Delta(t)=u_j$ for $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$; its value at $T$ is immaterial in $L^2$. If $u_j\in U_c$ for every $j$, then $u^\Delta\in\mathcal U_c$. A mesh family is refining when its mesh sizes tend to zero.

**Inputs.** Supply pointwise smooth data on $[0,T]$ from [[def-ctrl1-smooth-transcription-data]], an original mesh, a piecewise-constant control parameterization, an explicit tableau from [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] or a possibly implicit tableau from [[def-ctrl1-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-collocation]], one of `single-shooting`, `multiple-shooting`, or `collocation` mode, a finite smooth representation of the control constraints when a solver-ready NLP is requested, finite sets of declared path-constraint times, endpoint constraints, the tableau quadrature rule, an initial decision vector $z_0$ and multiplier vector $\mu_0$, a stage residual tolerance $\tau_s\ge0$, a quadrature error tolerance $\tau_q\ge0$, a stage Newton correction cap $M_s\in\mathbb N_0$, and a maximum number of mesh nodes. For the direct linear-stage branch, optionally supply exact pointwise coefficient maps $A:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $B:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ satisfying $f(t,x,u)=A(t)x+B(t)u$ at every queried stage input; only this explicit representation enables that branch. Supply a deterministic derivative evaluator for the actual returned stage maps and resulting finite NLP on an open neighborhood of the queried candidate. On a locally fixed strict stopping branch of the finite stage-iteration procedure, differentiate that finite graph, including when the residual happens to be exactly zero at the queried point. Implicit differentiation as in [[thm-implicit-differentiation-forward-and-adjoint-formulas]] is permitted only when the selected returned stage map is certified to agree on that neighborhood with the exact local solution branch and its residual Jacobian is nonsingular there; an exact residual at the queried point alone does not establish this agreement. Return `derivative-failure` when no derivative of the actual returned map is available. Supply a quadrature error evaluator which returns a certified upper bound for the objective quadrature discrepancy or `unavailable`. Each supplied evaluator returns a value or failure in finite time. An optional trajectory-estimation request supplies the inputs of [[alg-bounded-adaptive-runge-kutta-controller]].
$$X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_{k<i}a_{ik}F_{j,k},\quad t_{j,i}=t_j+c_ih_j,\quad F_{j,i}=f(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j),\quad \Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iF_{j,i}.$$

**Mesh and constraints.** Check that the original mesh satisfies $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ and that all declared constraint and quadrature times lie in $[0,T]$; if either check fails, return `mesh-domain-failure` without evaluation. If the original node count exceeds the supplied cap, return `mesh-budget-exhausted`. Insert every declared path-constraint time not already a node, unless this exceeds the node cap, in which case return `mesh-budget-exhausted`. Tie each inserted subcell's control to its original containing cell, so the parameterization is unchanged. On the resulting mesh, check all stage times $t_j+c_i h_j$ lie in $[0,T]$ before querying $f$ or $L$; an invalid time returns `mesh-domain-failure` with no evaluation. Each tableau stage and its quadrature contribution use the control $u_j$ of that cell, as in the stage equations below. At a declared path- or endpoint-constraint time that is a mesh node before $T$, use the right-hand original-cell value from the half-open representative in [[def-ctrl1-control-mesh-and-piecewise-constant-parameterization]]; at $T$, use the last original-cell control value unless a separate endpoint-control variable is supplied. Use the same convention at separately declared non-stage quadrature times. An endpoint constraint is evaluated at its declared endpoint. This is finite sampling and does not assert continuous-path feasibility.

**Stage evaluation.** On each cell write $h_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$ and $u_j$ for its tied constant control. Before forming any stages, check $X_{j,0}\in\Omega_x$ and $u_j\in\Omega_u$; a failed check returns `stage-domain-failure` with the cell and no objective candidate. For an explicit tableau, form the stages recursively by the displayed equations. Before each query of $f$ or $L$, check that the time is in $[0,T]$, the state lies in $\Omega_x$, and the control lies in $\Omega_u$; a failed membership check returns `stage-domain-failure`, and an unavailable function value returns `stage-evaluation-failure` with the cell and stage index. Apply the same checks to every declared path-constraint evaluation.

For an implicit tableau, do not leave the collocation stages as outer NLP decision variables. Form the coupled slope residual
$$R_j(K;X_{j,0},u_j)_i=K_i-f\!\left(t_j+c_ih_j,X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k,u_j\right),\quad i=1,\ldots,s.$$
With the stage times fixed and already checked in $[0,T]$, its open evaluation domain consists of stage vectors for which every induced stage state lies in $\Omega_x$ and the cell control lies in $\Omega_u$; require $R_j$ to be $C^1$ on this domain. A compact tube used for bounds does not replace this open evaluation domain. If exact coefficient maps $A,B$ were supplied and satisfy $f(t,x,u)=A(t)x+B(t)u$ at every queried stage input, form the finite matrix $M_j$ with blocks $(M_j)_{ik}=\delta_{ik}I-h_ja_{ik}A(t_{j,i})$ and right-hand side $r_i=A(t_{j,i})X_{j,0}+B(t_{j,i})u_j$. Use exact Gaussian elimination on the stored sample coefficients: scan columns left to right, pivot on the first nonzero entry at or below the current row, swap, eliminate below, and back-substitute. If no pivot is available, return `singular-stage-matrix`; otherwise form every induced stage state and check every stage time-state-control input belongs to the smooth-data tube. A failed domain check returns `stage-domain-failure` with the failing cell and stage index, the partial result record, and no objective candidate. If all checks pass, the exact solution of $M_jK=r$ is the stage vector and the nonlinear-solve status is `exact-linear-stage-solve`. In all other smooth cases, form the deterministic initial guess $K_i^{(0)}=f(t_j,X_{j,0},u_j)$ after checking that this query is defined. Before calling Newton, check that the entire seed $K^{(0)}$ belongs to the declared open domain of $R_j$, equivalently that every induced stage state lies in $\Omega_x$ and every required control lies in $\Omega_u$. If this check fails, return `stage-domain-failure` with the failing cell and stage index, the partial result record, and no objective candidate. Otherwise call [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] on $R_j$ with that open evaluation domain, tolerance $\tau_s$ and cap $M_s$. Record its iterate, residual vector, and exact status for each cell. Only `root` supplies a stage candidate; it means $\|R_j\|_2\le\tau_s$, not an exact root unless $\tau_s=0$. Any other status returns the partial result record with `nlp_status=stage-solve-failure`, the failing cell, and no objective candidate. On a returned stage vector use $X_{j,i}=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_k a_{ik}K_k$ and $\Phi_j=X_{j,0}+h_j\sum_i b_iK_i$. A singular stage Jacobian or failed stage query is reported, not interpreted as lack of an exact solution.

**Transcription modes.** In single shooting, the decision variables are the original-cell controls; set $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and recursively compute $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In multiple shooting, the decision variables are node states and controls; fix $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and impose the continuity equalities $d_j=X_{j+1,0}-\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)=0$ for $j=0,\ldots,N-1$. In collocation mode, use the same node/control variables, impose the same continuity equalities $d_j=0$, and use solved internal stage states; the collocation equations are solved internally by the implicit-stage procedure above. Explicit stages are likewise internal deterministic evaluations. After every interval map in every mode, check $\Phi_j\in\Omega_x$ before using it as a later start or evaluating a path constraint, terminal cost, or endpoint constraint; otherwise return `stage-domain-failure` with no objective candidate. Independently of the computed endpoints and defect residuals, check $X_{N,0}\in\Omega_x$ before evaluating $\phi(X_{N,0})$ or any terminal constraint; in multiple shooting and collocation this node is an independent decision variable even when $\Phi_{N-1}\in\Omega_x$. Before any endpoint-constraint query, also check every actual state and control argument, including a separately supplied endpoint-control variable, belongs to that function's declared domain. Any failed membership check returns `stage-domain-failure` with no objective candidate. In every mode the finite feasible set includes $u_j\in U_c$ for each original cell. The finite objective is $\sum_j h_j\sum_i b_iL(t_{j,i},X_{j,i},u_j)+\phi(X_{N,0})$, and the finite constraints are exactly the fixed initial-state condition, the continuity equalities $d_j=0$ in multiple shooting and collocation, the declared node/time constraints, the represented control constraints, and endpoint constraints. Include every continuity defect in the equality residual $h$ and its corresponding multiplier in $\nu$; in single shooting the initial state and continuity are enforced by recursive elimination. If $U_c$ is available only as a compact set-membership constraint and has no finite smooth representation, return the finite set-constrained model with `nlp_status=not-smooth-nlp`; the dispatcher must not treat it as an SQP-ready NLP. A QP solver route additionally requires the sampled control constraints to be affine.

**Output.** Evaluate the supplied initial candidate and return a record containing its ordered decision variables, defect residuals, per-cell implicit-stage residuals, path/endpoint constraint residuals, KKT residuals, and objective value, when available. For equality residual $h$, inequality residual $g\le0$, and multiplier pair $(\nu,\lambda)$, report $r_p=(h,[g]_+)$, $r_d=\nabla J_N+Dh^T\nu+Dg^T\lambda$, $r_\lambda=[-\lambda]_+$, and $r_c=\lambda\odot g$. Include a model that can reevaluate these quantities at a later solver candidate. Return separate `nlp_status`, per-cell `implicit_stage_status`, optional `ivp_status`, `quadrature_status`, `mesh_status`, and `budget_status` fields. A quadrature bound at most $\tau_q$ is `bound-met`; a larger bound is `bound-not-met`; an unavailable bound is `unavailable`. The build-stage budget field is `not-run`; the solver dispatcher fills its final value. A failed derivative evaluation leaves KKT residuals unavailable with its exact status. An unevaluated optional IVP estimate is `not-requested`; if requested, report the adaptive controller's exact finite status, not an error certificate.

This direct transcription samples pointwise data; an $L^\infty$ equivalence class without a chosen representative and sampling rule is not stage-evaluable. For a single-shooting reduced objective represented as the finite state-step graph of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]], its exact real-arithmetic reduced gradient is given by [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]. Agreement with the continuous ODE adjoint gradient is only conditional on the weighted discrete-gradient representation and the separate state, adjoint, derivative-data, endpoint, and quadrature estimates in [[thm-discrete-continuous-gradient-error-order-p]]. The optional adaptive RK estimate is separate from the fixed NLP and its embedded difference is not a certified global error bound. If all construction, stage, sample-domain and objective checks succeed, return `nlp_status=constructed` for a solver-ready NLP, or `nlp_status=not-smooth-nlp` for a finite set-constrained model without a smooth control representation; set `mesh_status=valid` and retain `budget_status=not-run`. The algorithm makes no continuous-path feasibility, convergence-rate, global-optimality, or unconditioned discrete-adjoint accuracy claim.

Fix a mesh, controls $u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}$, and a successful deterministic Runge–Kutta interval map $\Phi_j$ from [[alg-ctrl1-runge-kutta-shooting-and-collocation-transcription]]. In the single-shooting NLP, define states recursively from $X_{0,0}=x_0$ and $X_{j+1,0}=\Phi_j(X_{j,0},u_j)$. In the multiple-shooting NLP, impose the same initial state and continuity equations. Then projection from the multiple-shooting feasible set onto its control coordinates is a bijection onto the single-shooting feasible controls. Any objective and node constraints that use the same recursively determined states have identical reduced values and feasibility. This is an algebraic equivalence of the discrete NLPs; it is not an equivalence to the continuous ODE problem.

derivations.claim: On the first cell every stage slope equals $v_0$, so its endpoint increment is $\frac12v_0\sum_i b_i=\frac12v_0$. The second cell adds $\frac12v_1\sum_i b_i=\frac12v_1$. Thus single shooting gives the stated $x_1$ and $x_2$.

The multiple-shooting continuity equations uniquely impose $x_1=\frac12v_0$ and $x_2=x_1+\frac12v_1=\frac12(v_0+v_1)$. Substitution into its objective gives exactly the single-shooting objective. This is the concrete bijection and reduced-objective identity stated in [F3].

citations.quote:
Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

For $a\le b$, every gauge on a compact interval admits a fine tagged partition.

Equivalently, every gauge admits a fine tagged partition, and every gauge admits at least one fine tagged partition. In particular, every gauge on each complementary compact interval admits a fine tagged partition.

Let $a\le b$. A **gauge** on $[a,b]$ is a function $\delta:[a,b]\to(0,\infty)$. A tagged partition is written

$$P=\{([x_{i-1},x_i],\xi_i):1\le i\le m\},$$

where $a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b$ and $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$. It is **$\delta$-fine** when

$$[x_{i-1},x_i]\subset(\xi_i-\delta(\xi_i),\xi_i+\delta(\xi_i))$$

for every $i$. Its Riemann sum is $S(f,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m f(\xi_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$.

When $a=b$, the single degenerate tagged cell $([a,a],a)$ is declared a fine tagged partition for every gauge, and its Riemann sum is $0$. A **fine partial tagged partition** is any finite pairwise interior-disjoint family of cells $([u_j,v_j],\xi_j)$ with $[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, $u_j\le v_j$, and $\xi_j\in[u_j,v_j]$, each satisfying the same gauge-containment condition. The empty family is allowed and has sum $0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For **every** subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
measurable or not,

$$\lambda_n^*(E) \;=\; \inf\,\{\, \lambda_n(U) \;:\; U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ open and } E \subseteq U \,\},$$

the infimum being taken in $[0,+\infty]$ over a family that is nonempty because
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is open.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$. **Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then Lebesgue outer measure $\lambda_n^*$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]) is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-outer-measure]]): it vanishes at $\varnothing$, is monotone, and is
countably subadditive.

**The agreement clause is a theorem of ZF and needs no choice principle:**
$\lambda_n^*(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$
([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]), where $\mu_0$ is elementary volume. In
particular $\lambda_n^*(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
and $\lambda_n^*(\varnothing) = 0$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, both conclusions hold directly. Otherwise fix $a\le s<t\le b$ and $\varepsilon>0$ for claim 1. Let $E$ be a null exceptional set for $F'=0$ on $[s,t]$, enlarged by $s,t$; it is null by [F4]. Restricting [F1] to $[s,t]$, choose $d>0$ so that total interval length below $d$ implies total absolute increment below $\varepsilon/2$. Put $\eta=\varepsilon/(2(t-s+1))$. By [F3], choose one open $U\supseteq E$ with $\lambda(U)<d$.

For $x\notin E$, define $k(x)$ as the least $k\in\mathbb N_0$ such that $|F(y)-F(x)|\le\eta|y-x|$ whenever $y\in[s,t]$ and $|y-x|<2^{-k}$. This set is nonempty by $F'(x)=0$, [F7] and [F5], including $y=x$ by equality. For $x\in E$, instead take the least $k$ with $(x-2^{-k},x+2^{-k})\subseteq U$; openness and [F5] give existence. Set $\gamma(x)=2^{-k(x)}$. These uniquely specified least integers define one positive gauge; no arbitrary pointwise radius selections are needed. Obtain one finite $\gamma$-fine partition $\{([x_{i-1},x_i],\xi_i)\}_{i=1}^m$ from [F2].

Cells tagged in $E$ lie in $U$. Their interiors are disjoint, and their total length is the measure of their finite union, since shared endpoints form a finite null set. By [F4] this sum is at most $\lambda(U)<d$, so [F1] bounds their total absolute $F$-increment by $\varepsilon/2$; for an empty family the sum is zero.

For every other cell, strict fineness and step 2.1 give $|F(x_i)-F(x_{i-1})|\le|F(x_i)-F(\xi_i)|+|F(\xi_i)-F(x_{i-1})|\le\eta(x_i-x_{i-1})$, because the tag lies in the cell. The sum over these cells is at most $\eta(t-s)<\varepsilon/2$. Telescoping all cells and applying step 3.1 yields $|F(t)-F(s)|<\varepsilon$. Arbitrary positive $\varepsilon$ gives equality, and arbitrary $s,t$ prove claim 1.

For claim 2 with $a<b$, fix a coordinate $j$ and put $I_j(t)=\int_a^t h_j(s)\,ds$. By [F6], $I_j$ is absolutely continuous and $I'_j=h_j$ almost everywhere. The function $H_j=y_j-y_j(a)-I_j$ is absolutely continuous: for each positive tolerance use the [F1] moduli for $y_j,I_j$ at half that tolerance and take their minimum. Outside the union of the two exceptional null sets, [F7] gives $H'_j=0$. Claim 1 makes $H_j$ constant, and $H_j(a)=0$, so $y_j(t)=y_j(a)+I_j(t)$ for all $t$. Applying this argument to the finitely many coordinates proves the displayed vector identity.

risk_review.notes: Read all five proof steps and exact statements of all 13 suppliers. The least dyadic radius is uniquely specified at good and exceptional tags; Cousin supplies a finite fine partition without pointwise choice. Bad-tag cells lie in one open null cover of measure below the absolute-continuity modulus; good-tag increments sum to eta(t-s)<epsilon/2. Finite shared endpoints are null. Subtracting the indefinite L1 integral leaves an absolutely continuous function with zero derivative off a finite null union, yielding reconstruction coordinatewise. Countable Choice covers outer regularity and the first L1 FTC; a=b and empty bad-cell families are handled. This is a complete local gauge argument, independent of stronger differentiability/reconstruction theorems.
